title: agios
summary: Leviticus 19 calls Israel to holiness because the Lord is holy, and Isaiah 6 depicts the seraphim proclaiming the Lord’s holiness. First Peter 1 cites the command from Leviticus as a call to its readers; Hebrews 12 urges them to pursue holiness. The passages link God’s character with a community’s way of life. The Hebrew-scripture references provide context for the New Testament texts, but the set should not be treated as though each passage uses the same original-language word.
historical_context: The references include instruction in Leviticus, Isaiah’s vision, and exhortation in 1 Peter and Hebrews. The later letters draw on Israel’s Scriptures in addressing their readers; these textual relationships are clear without an external history of the term.
canonical_context: Leviticus grounds Israel’s call in God’s holiness. Isaiah’s vision emphasizes the holiness of the Lord, while 1 Peter explicitly recalls the scriptural command and Hebrews urges pursuit of holiness. The group connects divine holiness and faithful conduct across different settings.
literary_context: Leviticus gives a command, Isaiah narrates a vision, 1 Peter draws on a scriptural quotation, and Hebrews exhorts its readers. The forms explain the different emphasis: holiness is commanded, seen, recalled, and pursued.
covenantal_significance: The passages connect belonging to God with a life shaped by God’s holiness. Leviticus gives the command to Israel; 1 Peter applies that scriptural call to its audience; Hebrews emphasizes the pursuit of holiness. The relationship is canonical and textual, not a claim that all passages provide a single definition.
canonical_role: This entry follows holiness from Israel’s instruction and prophetic vision into New Testament exhortation. Its references show how later writers draw on Israel’s Scriptures while addressing their own communities.

interpretive_notes.note: Do not reduce agios to a single English gloss.
Check the immediate context and genre before drawing theological conclusions.
